_note: Landmark criminal-law judgments with good-law status. status: good_law | overruled | partly_overruled | superseded. status_note says by what. Curated 2026-07-20; holdings are settled landmarks. The RAG doc text carries the status so the model can warn when a cited case is no longer good law.

judgments.case: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.
judgments.status_note: Binding Constitution Bench law.
judgments.ratio: Registration of FIR is MANDATORY under (then) CrPC 154 — now BNSS 173 — if the information discloses a cognizable offence; preliminary inquiry is permissible only in limited categories (matrimonial, commercial, medical negligence, corruption, abnormal delay) and must conclude within 7 (extended to 14) days.
judgments.practice: Cite when police refuse to register an FIR; pair with the writ/complaint remedy under BNSS 175(3).

judgments.case: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
judgments.status_note: Reaffirmed and extended by Satender Kumar Antil (2022).
judgments.ratio: For offences punishable up to 7 years, arrest is not to be made routinely; police must record reasons under (then) CrPC 41 — now BNSS 35 — and issue a notice of appearance (now BNSS 35(3)); Magistrates must not authorise detention mechanically.
judgments.practice: The shield against automatic arrest in matrimonial-cruelty (BNS 85) and similar sub-7-year cases.

judgments.case: Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI
judgments.status_note: Continuing mandamus; guidelines periodically enforced.
judgments.ratio: Comprehensive bail guidelines by offence category; bail applications to be decided within two weeks; Arnesh Kumar compliance mandatory; separate bail application not needed at chargesheet stage in some categories.
judgments.practice: The master bail-guidelines citation alongside BNSS 480-483.

judgments.case: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
judgments.status_note: Guidelines largely codified into CrPC 41B/50/54 — now BNSS 36/47/53.
judgments.ratio: Eleven mandatory safeguards on arrest and detention: identification of officers, arrest memo with witness, right to inform a relative, medical examination, etc. Breach invites contempt and departmental action.
judgments.practice: Custodial-violence and illegal-detention matters; habeas corpus support.

judgments.case: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
judgments.status_note: The seven quashing categories remain the standard.
judgments.ratio: Seven categories where FIR/proceedings can be quashed under (then) CrPC 482 — now BNSS 528: no offence disclosed, absurd allegations, legal bar, mala fide prosecution, etc.
judgments.practice: The foundation of every quashing petition.

judgments.case: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab
judgments.status_note: Followed in Narinder Singh (2014) and Laxmi Narayan (2019).
judgments.ratio: High Court may quash non-compoundable offences of a private/civil flavour on settlement under inherent powers, but not heinous offences (murder, rape, dacoity) or offences against the State.
judgments.practice: Settlement-based quashing of cheating/matrimonial FIRs.

judgments.case: Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi)
judgments.status_note: Overruled Salauddin Shaikh line requiring time-limited anticipatory bail.
judgments.ratio: Anticipatory bail (then CrPC 438 — now BNSS 482) need not be limited in time; it can continue till the end of trial unless cancelled.
judgments.practice: Oppose attempts to time-limit anticipatory bail.

judgments.case: Salauddin Abdulsamad Shaikh v. State of Maharashtra
judgments.status_note: OVERRULED by Sushila Aggarwal (2020) (Constitution Bench) — anticipatory bail need not be time-bound.
judgments.ratio: (Historical) Anticipatory bail should be of limited duration, leaving the regular court to decide bail.
judgments.practice: Do NOT cite for time-limiting anticipatory bail — cite Sushila Aggarwal instead.

judgments.case: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
judgments.status_note: Settled the 65B conflict; overruled Shafhi Mohammad; clarified Anvar P.V.
judgments.ratio: The certificate under (then) IEA 65B(4) — now BSA 63(4) — is a condition precedent to admissibility of secondary electronic evidence; required unless the party is not in possession of the device; can be produced at trial with leave.
judgments.practice: Every WhatsApp-screenshot/CCTV-clip case: file the BSA 63 certificate.

judgments.case: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
judgments.status_note: Affirmed by Arjun Panditrao (2020); overruled Navjot Sandhu on the 65B point.
judgments.ratio: Electronic records are documentary evidence admissible only per the special procedure (then IEA 65A/65B — now BSA 62/63); the general secondary-evidence route is unavailable.
judgments.practice: Foundation authority for the electronic-evidence certificate regime.

judgments.case: Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh
judgments.status_note: OVERRULED by Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020) — the 65B certificate cannot be dispensed with on 'interest of justice' grounds.
judgments.ratio: (Historical) The 65B certificate requirement is procedural and can be relaxed where the device is not in the party's possession.
judgments.practice: Do NOT cite to avoid the BSA 63 certificate — cite Arjun Panditrao's possession exception instead.

judgments.case: State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu (Parliament Attack)
judgments.status_note: On electronic evidence (65B not mandatory) OVERRULED by Anvar P.V. (2014). Other holdings (conspiracy analysis) stand.
judgments.ratio: (Historical, on evidence) Secondary evidence of electronic records admissible under general provisions even without 65B certificate.
judgments.practice: Never cite for electronic-evidence admissibility.

judgments.case: Rajesh Sharma v. State of U.P.
judgments.status_note: Family Welfare Committee mechanism STRUCK OUT by Social Action Forum for Manav Adhikar (2018); other safeguards modified.
judgments.ratio: (Historical) Directed Family Welfare Committees to screen 498A complaints before arrest.
judgments.practice: Do NOT cite the committee mechanism; use Arnesh Kumar + Social Action Forum for 498A/BNS 85 arrest safeguards.

judgments.case: Social Action Forum for Manav Adhikar v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: Governs 498A/BNS 85 arrest practice with Arnesh Kumar.
judgments.ratio: Family Welfare Committees have no legal basis; protection against mechanical arrest in matrimonial-cruelty cases flows from CrPC 41/41A (now BNSS 35) discipline, anticipatory bail remains available.
judgments.practice: Pair with Arnesh Kumar in every BNS 85 defence advisory.

judgments.case: Satbir Singh v. State of Haryana
judgments.status_note: Current authority on dowry-death trials.
judgments.ratio: 'Soon before death' in (then) IPC 304B — now BNS 80 — means proximate and live link, not immediately before; once ingredients are shown the (now) BSA 118 presumption is mandatory; trial courts must examine the accused meaningfully under (now) BNSS 351.
judgments.practice: Dowry-death prosecutions: sequence of proof + presumption.

judgments.case: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra
judgments.status_note: The five golden principles (panchsheel) of circumstantial evidence.
judgments.ratio: Conviction on circumstantial evidence requires: fully established circumstances, consistent only with guilt, conclusive nature, exclusion of every hypothesis of innocence, and a complete chain.
judgments.practice: Defence framework in every circumstantial murder case.

judgments.case: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
judgments.status_note: Death-penalty framework; refined by Machhi Singh and Manoj (2022) mitigation guidelines.
judgments.ratio: Death sentence only in the 'rarest of rare' cases where the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed; aggravating and mitigating circumstances of both crime and criminal must be balanced.
judgments.practice: Sentencing hearings in capital matters (BNS 103, 66, 70(2)).

judgments.case: Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab
judgments.status_note: Operationalises Bachan Singh.
judgments.ratio: Five categories (manner, motive, magnitude, anti-social nature, victim status) to test whether a murder is rarest of rare.
judgments.practice: Both sides of capital sentencing argument.

judgments.case: Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab
judgments.status_note: Classic, constantly applied.
judgments.ratio: For murder under (then) IPC 300 thirdly — now within BNS 101 — prosecution must prove the bodily injury present, and that the injury intended was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; intention to cause that specific injury suffices.
judgments.practice: Murder vs culpable homicide line (BNS 101 vs 105).

judgments.case: Pulukuri Kottaya v. Emperor
judgments.status_note: Still the leading exposition of the discovery proviso.
judgments.ratio: Under (then) IEA 27 — now proviso to BSA 23(2) — only that part of the information which distinctly relates to the fact discovered is admissible; the fact discovered includes the place and the accused's knowledge, not the confessional content.
judgments.practice: Limit recovery-evidence to the discovery, exclude confessional surplus.

judgments.case: Aghnoo Nagesia v. State of Bihar
judgments.status_note: Standard authority on confessional FIRs.
judgments.ratio: A confessional FIR lodged by the accused with police is hit by (then) IEA 25 — now BSA 23(1) — in its entirety except the portion leading to discovery and non-confessional facts.
judgments.practice: Exclude confessional FIRs; salvage only discovery portions.

judgments.case: Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani
judgments.status_note: Expanded by Selvi (2010).
judgments.ratio: Article 20(3) protection against self-incrimination extends to the investigation stage; an accused may refuse to answer incriminating questions during police interrogation (now BNSS 180 examinations).
judgments.practice: Advising clients summoned for interrogation.

judgments.case: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
judgments.status_note: Governs narco/polygraph/BEAP.
judgments.ratio: Involuntary narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping violate Article 20(3) and personal liberty; results admissible only if the technique was consented to, and even then only discoveries made in consequence are usable.
judgments.practice: Oppose involuntary forensic-psychological tests.

judgments.case: Ritesh Sinha v. State of U.P.
judgments.status_note: Voice samples; BNSS 349 now codifies specimen powers.
judgments.ratio: A Magistrate can direct an accused to give voice samples for investigation even without express statutory provision; does not violate Article 20(3).
judgments.practice: Voice-sample directions in extortion/bribery tapes.

judgments.case: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: IT Act 66A void ab initio; Zombie-prosecution directions in 2021-22 followups.
judgments.ratio: IT Act Section 66A struck down as unconstitutionally vague and overbroad; intermediary liability under 79 read down to actual-knowledge via court/government order.
judgments.practice: Any prosecution citing IT Act 66A is void — seek immediate quashing.

judgments.case: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: Adultery (IPC 497) unconstitutional; BNS contains no adultery offence.
judgments.ratio: IPC 497 (adultery) struck down as violative of Articles 14, 15 and 21; adultery may be a ground for divorce but not a crime.
judgments.practice: Adultery allegations have civil (divorce) consequences only.

judgments.case: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: IPC 377 read down; BNS omits the offence for consenting adults.
judgments.ratio: IPC 377 unconstitutional insofar as it criminalised consensual sexual acts between adults; non-consensual acts and acts with minors remain punishable (now via BNS sexual-offence and POCSO provisions).
judgments.practice: Consensual same-sex relations are no offence; non-consensual acts charge under BNS 63-70/POCSO.

judgments.case: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: Privacy is a fundamental right; the DPDP Act 2023 operates under it.
judgments.ratio: Privacy is intrinsic to Article 21; State intrusion requires legality, necessity and proportionality.
judgments.practice: Surveillance, phone-tapping, data-seizure challenges; DPDP compliance framing.

judgments.case: Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab
judgments.status_note: Overruled P. Rathinam; note Mental Healthcare Act 2017 s.115 presumes severe stress in attempted suicide; BNS has no general attempt-to-suicide offence (only BNS 226 attempt to compel a public servant).
judgments.ratio: Right to life under Article 21 does not include a right to die; (then) IPC 306 abetment of suicide — now BNS 108 — is constitutionally valid.
judgments.practice: Abetment-of-suicide prosecutions under BNS 108.

judgments.case: P. Rathinam v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: OVERRULED by Gian Kaur (1996) Constitution Bench.
judgments.ratio: (Historical) IPC 309 attempt to suicide held unconstitutional as violating Article 21.
judgments.practice: Do not cite; the constitutional analysis is Gian Kaur's.

judgments.case: Mohan Lal v. State of Punjab
judgments.status_note: OVERRULED by Mukesh Singh v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2020) Constitution Bench — informant-investigator overlap is not automatically fatal.
judgments.ratio: (Historical) A fair investigation requires that the informant and the investigator not be the same person; such trials stood vitiated.
judgments.practice: Cite Mukesh Singh (2020): overlap goes to weight, decided case-by-case.

judgments.case: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab
judgments.status_note: Now reflected in BNS 106(1)'s reduced punishment for registered medical practitioners.
judgments.ratio: Criminal prosecution of doctors for negligence requires gross negligence (recklessness), supported by credible expert opinion; simple lack of care attracts only civil liability.
judgments.practice: Medical-negligence FIR defence; BNS 106(1) proviso (2 years for registered practitioners).

judgments.case: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar
judgments.status_note: Speedy-trial right; operationalised today via BNSS 479 undertrial release.
judgments.ratio: Speedy trial is an essential ingredient of Article 21; undertrials detained beyond the maximum possible sentence must be released.
judgments.practice: Undertrial release petitions (now BNSS 479 makes 1/3 for first offenders statutory).

judgments.case: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: Foundation of modern Article 21 jurisprudence.
judgments.ratio: Procedure established by law under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable; Articles 14, 19 and 21 interlock.
judgments.practice: Constitutional backbone for procedural challenges.

judgments.case: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
judgments.status_note: SUPERSEDED by the POSH Act 2013 — the Vishaka guidelines now operate through the statute; cite the Act, not the guidelines.
judgments.ratio: (Historical) Laid binding guidelines on prevention of sexual harassment at the workplace until legislation was enacted.
judgments.practice: Workplace sexual-harassment matters proceed under the POSH Act 2013 + BNS 75.

judgments.case: Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar
judgments.status_note: IPC 124A (sedition) suspended by S.G. Vombatkere v. UoI (2022) and then REPEALED by the BNS; the successor offence is BNS 152 with a lawful-criticism explanation.
judgments.ratio: (Historical) Sedition upheld but confined to acts with tendency to incite violence or public disorder.
judgments.practice: Sedition FIRs post-2024 must be tested against BNS 152, not 124A; Kedar Nath's incitement threshold remains persuasive for 152.

judgments.case: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: Internet-shutdown and Section 144 review standards.
judgments.ratio: Orders under (then) CrPC 144 — now BNSS 163 — must state material facts, be proportionate, and are subject to judicial review; indefinite internet suspension is impermissible.
judgments.practice: Challenging prohibitory orders and internet shutdowns.

judgments.case: Lily Thomas v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: With Sarla Mudgal (1995).
judgments.ratio: Conversion to another religion solely to contract a second marriage does not dissolve the first; the second marriage is void and attracts bigamy (then IPC 494 — now BNS 82).
judgments.practice: Bigamy-by-conversion prosecutions under BNS 82.

judgments.case: Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma
judgments.status_note: Live-in relationships under the DV Act.
judgments.ratio: Guidelines on when a live-in relationship is a 'relationship in the nature of marriage' attracting the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005.
judgments.practice: DV Act claims arising from live-in relationships, alongside BNS 85 where applicable.

judgments.case: Independent Thought v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: Carried into BNS 63 Exception 2 (age raised to 18).
judgments.ratio: Sexual intercourse by a husband with a wife below 18 is rape; the marital exception cannot dilute the age of consent.
judgments.practice: Child-marriage-related sexual offence prosecutions (BNS 63-65 + POCSO).

judgments.case: Mukesh v. State (NCT of Delhi) (Nirbhaya)
judgments.status_note: Death sentences executed 2020.
judgments.ratio: Affirmed capital sentence in a gang-rape-murder as rarest of rare; dying declarations (three, consistent) and electronic/DNA evidence sustained conviction.
judgments.practice: Template for multi-declarant dying declarations and forensic corroboration (BNS 70(2), BSA 26).

judgments.case: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra
judgments.status_note: Grave-and-sudden-provocation classic.
judgments.ratio: The provocation exception requires loss of self-control that is both grave and sudden; premeditated retrieval of a weapon and confrontation defeats the exception.
judgments.practice: Testing Exception 1 to murder (now within BNS 101 exceptions).

judgments.case: Pakala Narayana Swami v. Emperor
judgments.status_note: Perennial authority on dying declarations and confessions.
judgments.ratio: 'Circumstances of the transaction resulting in death' under (then) IEA 32(1) — now BSA 26(a) — includes statements about events with proximate relation to death; a confession must either admit guilt or substantially all facts constituting the offence.
judgments.practice: Scope arguments on dying declarations (BSA 26).

judgments.case: Laxman v. State of Maharashtra
judgments.status_note: Settled the certification conflict.
judgments.ratio: A dying declaration is not invalid merely because the doctor's fitness certificate is absent; what matters is the court's satisfaction that the declarant was fit and the statement voluntary and truthful.
judgments.practice: Defending/attacking dying declarations without medical certification (BSA 26).

judgments.case: Hanumant Govind Nargundkar v. State of M.P.
judgments.status_note: Origin of the circumstantial-evidence standard later crystallised in Sharad Sarda.
judgments.ratio: Circumstances must be fully established and the chain so complete as to exclude every reasonable hypothesis except guilt.
judgments.practice: Read with Sharad Sarda in circumstantial cases.

judgments.case: Tuka Ram v. State of Maharashtra (Mathura)
judgments.status_note: SUPERSEDED by the 1983 amendment (custodial rape, consent presumption — then IEA 114A, now BSA 120) enacted in response; its consent reasoning is no longer law.
judgments.ratio: (Historical) Acquittal in custodial rape for absence of injuries/'passive submission' — triggered nationwide reform.
judgments.practice: Cite only as history; the law is BSA 120's consent presumption in custodial/aggravated rape.

judgments.case: Rambraksh v. State of Chhattisgarh
judgments.status_note: Representative of the settled last-seen line (with Satpal 2018).
judgments.ratio: Last-seen-together evidence alone, without proximity of time and corroboration, is insufficient for murder conviction; BSA 109 (fact especially within knowledge) does not relieve the prosecution of its primary burden.
judgments.practice: Defence in last-seen circumstantial cases.

judgments.case: Prakash Singh v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: Police-reform directions; compliance still monitored.
judgments.ratio: Seven binding directives on police reform: State Security Commissions, fixed tenure, separation of investigation from law-and-order, Police Complaints Authorities.
judgments.practice: Complaints against police via the Police Complaints Authority route.

judgments.case: Youth Bar Association of India v. Union of India
judgments.status_note: Now codified in BNSS 173(3)/193 disclosure norms.
judgments.ratio: Copies of FIRs must be uploaded on police/state websites within 24 hours (48-72 for remote areas), except sensitive categories; accused entitled to FIR copy before appearing.
judgments.practice: Getting FIR copies quickly; challenging non-upload.

judgments.case: Sakiri Vasu v. State of U.P.
judgments.status_note: The 156(3) remedial ladder.
judgments.ratio: If police refuse FIR or investigate improperly, the remedy ladder is: SP under (then) 154(3), then Magistrate under (then) 156(3) — now BNSS 175(3)-(4) — which includes all incidental powers to ensure proper investigation; writ petitions should not be the first resort.
judgments.practice: The standard escalation route for FIR refusal, after Lalita Kumari.

judgments.case: Vinubhai Haribhai Malaviya v. State of Gujarat
judgments.status_note: Magistrate's further-investigation power till chargesheet acceptance.
judgments.ratio: Magistrates have power under (then) 156(3) — now BNSS 175(3) — to order further investigation even after a chargesheet, until charges are framed.
judgments.practice: Seeking further investigation of shoddy chargesheets.
